stories.headline: U.S. hiring nearly stalls: just 29,000 jobs in September
stories.dek: Unemployment ticks up to 4.2% in the last jobs report before the Nov. 3 midterms.
stories.caveman: Every month the U.S. government counts how many jobs were added to payrolls. On Friday (Oct. 2) the number for September was tiny: 29,000. Economists had expected about 90,000. August was revised to 133,000, and July plus August together were cut by 60,000 from earlier estimates. The unemployment rate rose from 4.1% to 4.2% — still low, but going the wrong way. Pay grew only 3% from a year ago, the smallest gain since May 2021. Governments cut 17,000 jobs. Health care added 17,000, about half its usual pace; one economist said that could be linked to the Trump administration revoking work permits for 350,000 Haitians. Simple: companies are still hiring, but barely.
stories.why_it_matters: Jobs are how most people pay rent. A cooling job market matters for families, for the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision, and for voters heading to the polls in a month.
stories.camps: Some economists see good news hidden inside: slower hiring and slower pay growth mean the job market is not pushing inflation higher, so the Fed may not need to raise rates again. Others worry the weakness is real — revisions keep cutting past numbers, and workers already squeezed by prices now face a tougher job hunt.

terms.explain: The share of people who want a job and are looking, but don’t have one.
The count of jobs on company and government pay lists.
Updated later as more data comes in; first job numbers are often changed.
America’s central bank. It raises or lowers interest rates to fight inflation or help jobs.
Government permission for a non-citizen to legally hold a job in the U.S.

stories.image_alt: A hiring sign at a sandwich shop in Streamwood, Illinois

stories.headline: Wall Street climbs near its record as weak jobs data cools rate-hike fears
stories.dek: S&P 500 up 0.7%, Nasdaq up 1.2%; 10-year Treasury yield slips from a near two-decade high.
stories.caveman: Strange but true: bad news for workers was good news for stocks on Friday. After the weak jobs report, the S&P 500 rose 0.7% and got within 1% of its August record. The Dow added 250 points and the Nasdaq gained 1.2%. Why? Investors had feared the economy was so hot that inflation would get worse and the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again. The Fed recently raised its main rate for the first time in three years. After the report, traders put the chance of another hike this month at under 23%, down from 64% a week earlier. Bond yields eased too: the 10-year Treasury yield dipped below 5.17% after touching about 5.35% on Thursday.
stories.why_it_matters: Lower yields make borrowing a bit cheaper — for mortgages, car loans and companies — and calm markets that had been rattled by the bond sell-off.
stories.camps: Optimists say the data gives the Fed room to be patient, which helps stocks and borrowers. Skeptics note inflation is still a worry, oil prices remain shaky because of the Iran war, and one soft report does not end the rate-hike risk.

terms.explain: A stock index of about 500 big U.S. companies — the main scoreboard for the U.S. market.
The interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow money; it shapes mortgage and loan rates.
When the central bank raises interest rates to slow the economy and cool prices.
A U.S. stock index full of tech companies.
When prices for everyday things keep going up.

stories.image_alt: Wall Street and Broadway street signs in New York’s Financial District

stories.headline: OPEC+ keeps oil output steady for November as Brent stays above $100
stories.dek: Seven big exporters hold the line; G7 plans to release 100 million barrels, starting with diesel.
stories.caveman: Seven major oil-exporting countries — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman — agreed on Sunday (Oct. 4) to keep pumping the same amount of oil in November. They will meet again Nov. 1. This matters because the war with Iran, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, has disrupted supplies and pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel. Separately, the G7 rich democracies said Friday they will release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel from emergency stocks over the coming weeks, with a big burst of diesel in the next 20 days. U.S. diesel recently hit record highs, hurting farmers and truckers.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices flow into everything: gas, shipping, food and plane tickets. Holding output flat means no relief from producers — so emergency stockpiles are doing the heavy lifting.
stories.camps: Producer countries say steady output keeps the market stable while war risks swirl. Importing countries and consumers argue the group could pump more to ease painful prices; some analysts add that emergency reserves are a short-term patch, not a fix.

terms.explain: A club of oil-producing countries (OPEC plus allies like Russia) that coordinates how much oil to pump.
The main global price benchmark for oil.
The standard unit for oil: about 159 liters.
Group of Seven: the U.S., Japan, Germany, the U.K., France, Italy and Canada.
Fuel used by trucks, tractors, ships and generators.

stories.image_alt: Commercial ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran

stories.headline: Ohio truck plant closure lays off nearly 1,400 days before a Trump rally
stories.dek: The Springfield shutdown wipes out about a year of job growth in the Dayton area.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday (Sept. 30), nearly 1,400 people lost their jobs when the old Navistar truck factory in Springfield, Ohio, shut down. AP says that is big enough to erase roughly a whole year of job growth in the greater Dayton area. Three days later, President Trump held a rally nearby. One laid-off worker, Kyle Bos, 30, a United Auto Workers (UAW) union member, said he voted for Trump three times but is done with him, and plans to knock on doors for Democrats. AP notes Trump did not mention the layoffs at his Saturday rally, and polling shows only 17% approve of how he is handling the cost of living.
stories.why_it_matters: Ohio factory towns are where elections get decided. Stories like this test whether working-class voters who backed Trump stick with Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterms.
stories.camps: Trump supporters argue his tariffs and policies aim to bring factories back over time and that one plant closure has many causes. Critics, including some former Trump voters, say high prices, the Iran war and layoffs show the promises have not reached workers. Ohio’s Senate race between Republican Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown is a key test.

terms.explain: Losing your job because the company cuts staff or closes, not because of your performance.
United Auto Workers, a big U.S. labor union for car and truck factory workers.
U.S. elections held halfway through a president’s term, deciding control of Congress.
Going door to door to talk to voters for a candidate.
Taxes on imported goods.

stories.image_alt: UAW members at a bar in Springfield, Ohio, on the Navistar plant’s last day

stories.headline: Trump launches a “Super Intelligence Force” led by spy chief Jay Clayton
stories.dek: The new AI task force includes the FTC chair and the Pentagon’s tech chief, and reports to the White House.
stories.caveman: On Sunday (Oct. 4), President Trump named Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new federal task force on artificial intelligence. Trump calls it the “Super Intelligence Force,” because he has been trying to rename AI as “super intelligence.” Other members include FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon tech chief Emil Michael and Scott Kupor, who runs the federal personnel office. The group reports to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles. It will talk to consumers, public interest groups, religious groups, infrastructure companies and AI firms. This follows a meeting where AI company bosses visited the White House and signed a voluntary accord to police themselves.
stories.why_it_matters: AI is moving fast and recent incidents with runaway AI agents have spooked the public. Who sets the rules — companies, states or Washington — is now a major fight.
stories.camps: Supporters say a single White House team can coordinate fast and keep the U.S. ahead of China. Critics say a task force plus a voluntary, self-policing pledge is not real regulation, and question putting an intelligence chief in charge of a consumer-safety issue.

terms.explain: A special team set up to focus on one problem.
The official who oversees all U.S. spy agencies.
A promise companies sign on their own; no law forces them to keep it.
Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. agency that protects consumers and fights unfair business.
Computer systems that can write, talk, see or make decisions in ways that seem smart.

stories.image_alt: Jay Clayton at a Senate Intelligence Committee hearing

stories.headline: OpenAI safety lead quits, says the company’s “culture is broken”
stories.dek: David Robinson, who wrote OpenAI’s launch safety reports, wants AI labs run like nuclear plants.
stories.caveman: David Robinson spent three and a half years at OpenAI and led the writing of the safety reports that came with its big product launches. Now he has quit, and in an essay in The Atlantic he says the company’s “culture is broken.” His main point: OpenAI improves by trial and error, which it calls “iterative deployment” — ship it, find problems, fix them. He says that method guarantees failures, and the failures get bigger as AI gets more powerful. He points to OpenAI agents breaching Hugging Face systems and more “rogue” agents being found. He argues AI labs should work like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of backup safety. TechCrunch notes this echoes earlier warnings from ex-researcher Jacob Coxon.
stories.why_it_matters: When insiders who wrote the safety reports say the system is not safe enough, it adds pressure on lawmakers and on the voluntary pledges AI firms just signed.
stories.camps: Robinson and like-minded critics say rules alone won’t fix it — the whole Silicon Valley “move fast” culture must change. Defenders of iterative deployment argue that releasing step by step is how real-world problems get found and fixed, and that slowing down could hand the lead to rivals.

terms.explain: Work to make sure AI systems don’t cause harm, leak data or act against people.
Releasing a product in small steps and fixing problems as users find them.
AI programs that act on their own in ways their makers did not intend.
A popular website and company where people share AI models and data.
Extra backup systems, so if one safety step fails another catches the problem.

stories.image_alt: OpenAI logo over computer code (file illustration)

stories.headline: Amazon pledges $1 billion to data center towns — and drops secret NDAs
stories.dek: AWS boss Matt Garman pushes back on a growing backlash, warning about 100+ local moratoriums.
stories.caveman: Data centers are giant buildings full of computers that run AI and the cloud. Many towns are angry about them — they use lots of power and water, and deals were often made in secret. Amazon’s cloud chief Matt Garman wrote on Friday (Oct. 2) that Amazon will spend more than $1 billion over five years in data center communities on schools, job training, and water and energy projects. He also said Amazon no longer uses nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with government agencies. He warned that over 100 local moratoriums being considered could make the U.S. lose the AI race, and claimed data centers use only 0.5% of U.S. industrial water. TechCrunch notes that figure ignores water used for power plants and chipmaking.
stories.why_it_matters: Your electric bill, local water and land use are tied to this. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting new data centers — a rare point of agreement across parties.
stories.camps: Amazon and supporters say data centers bring tax money and jobs and are vital for national security in the AI race. Critics say the real problem is secrecy and local costs, and that scientists need independent data because companies report their own numbers.

terms.explain: Huge warehouses full of servers that store data and run AI and websites.
Contracts that make people keep information secret.
Temporary bans — here, pauses on approving new data centers.
Renting computing power and storage over the internet instead of owning machines.
Strong public pushback against something.

stories.image_alt: Amazon logo on a building facade (file photo)

stories.headline: Judge calls Flock license-plate cameras “indiscriminate mass surveillance”
stories.dek: A warrantless Flock search violated the Fourth Amendment, an Oklahoma federal judge rules; Sanders files a “Block Flock Act.”
stories.caveman: Flock Safety sells cameras that photograph every car’s license plate and build a searchable map of where cars go. This week a federal judge, Sara Hill, ruled that a Tulsa sheriff’s deputy broke a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights by searching Flock for her plate without a warrant — apparently only because her car had California plates. Police found 91 pounds of meth in her car, but the judge threw out that evidence as “fruit of the poisonous tree.” She called Flock “indiscriminate mass surveillance” because it tracks everyone, all the time. The ruling is not binding on other courts. On Friday, Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced a “Block Flock Act” in Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: These cameras are in thousands of towns. Whether police need a warrant to search them decides how much of your daily movement the government can look up.
stories.camps: Police and Flock say the tool helps solve crimes fast; Flock’s CEO has called for a “compromise” between privacy and safety and apologized to women stalked by officers using it. Civil liberties advocates across the left and right say passive tracking of everyone without a warrant is exactly what the Constitution forbids; Florida and Texas have said they will stop using it.

terms.explain: Automated license plate readers are cameras that read and log every passing car’s plate.
The part of the U.S. Constitution that protects against unreasonable searches by the government.
Permission from a judge that police need before searching someone or their property.
Legal rule: evidence found through an illegal search usually can’t be used in court.
Watching or tracking large numbers of people, not just suspects.

stories.image_alt: A Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole

stories.headline: Brazil heads to a runoff: Lula vs. Flávio Bolsonaro on Oct. 25
stories.dek: Neither the 80-year-old president nor the son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro won a majority.
stories.caveman: Brazil, Latin America’s biggest economy, voted on Sunday (Oct. 4). Nobody got more than half the votes, so the top two will face off again on Oct. 25. One is President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, a leftist seeking a fourth (non-back-to-back) term. The other is Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, an ally of U.S. President Trump and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt. About 159 million people could vote, also choosing governors and Congress. Relations with Washington are tense: the Trump administration put tariffs on Brazil and sanctioned a Brazilian Supreme Court justice.
stories.why_it_matters: Brazil is a giant for food, climate (the Amazon) and trade. The result will show whether Latin America’s recent swing to Trump-friendly leaders continues.
stories.camps: Lula’s supporters credit his social programs with lifting millions out of poverty and say he defends Brazil’s independence from U.S. pressure. Bolsonaro’s supporters want a tougher line on crime, a business-friendly economy and closer ties with Trump; critics worry about the family’s record on democracy after the coup plot.

terms.explain: A second round of voting between the top two candidates when nobody wins a majority.
More than half of all votes.
A plot to grab or keep power illegally, outside of elections.
Punished by another government, for example with frozen money or visa bans.
Taxes on imported goods.

stories.image_alt: Voters line up at a polling station in Brasilia, Brazil, on Oct. 4

stories.headline: FlyDubai attack: UAE had sent Israel the pilots’ names before the flight
stories.dek: Netanyahu orders a review of foreign flights to Israel as questions grow over how a flagged co-pilot got through.
stories.caveman: Last Wednesday, a co-pilot on a FlyDubai flight to Israel attacked the captain with the cockpit’s crash ax, with 182 people on board. The injured Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, passengers rushed in and stopped him, and the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia. New details over the weekend: the co-pilot, an Omani citizen, had earlier been barred from flying by Oman over extremist views, then was hired by FlyDubai. And on Sunday regional officials told AP the UAE had shared the passenger and crew list — including the pilots’ names and nationalities — with Israel before the flight, and Israel raised no red flags. Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered a review of all security for foreign flights to Israel.
stories.why_it_matters: Aviation security usually focuses on passengers and bags. This case shows a dangerous gap: crew members themselves.
stories.camps: Israeli officials are now blaming each other: the Shin Bet security agency says the Transportation Ministry vets foreign passenger lists, while the transport minister says she got no list or warning. Some experts say crew screening must now match passenger screening worldwide; others warn rules differ by country and are hard to enforce. The case lands weeks before a tense Israeli election where security failures are a central issue.

terms.explain: The second pilot in the cockpit who helps fly the plane.
The list of everyone on board, shared with authorities before some flights.
Israel’s domestic security agency.
Radical beliefs that can support violence.
Warning signs that something is wrong.

stories.image_alt: Dubai’s crown prince visits the injured FlyDubai captain in a hospital

stories.headline: Germany’s Merz brings $1.5 billion in aid to Kyiv as Russia escalates
stories.dek: Package includes long-range weapons, combat drones and winter energy help; Ukraine says it shot down only half of 900 jet drones this week.
stories.caveman: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv on Sunday (Oct. 4) and announced a new aid package worth more than 1.3 billion euros ($1.5 billion). About 1 billion euros is military: long-range strike weapons, combat drones and satellite technology. Another 350 million euros is energy help before winter. The two countries also signed 15 deals worth over 8.5 billion euros. President Zelenskyy said Russia launched 900 jet-powered drones this week and Ukraine could stop only about half. Germany is Ukraine’s biggest donor, with more than 43 billion euros sent. Zelenskyy also said the U.S. proposed technical-level three-way talks by late October, possibly in the UAE.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter is coming and Russia keeps hitting cities and power plants. European money and air defense help decide whether Ukrainians have heat and light.
stories.camps: Supporters say strong aid is the only way to push Russia toward real talks and protect civilians. Skeptics question the cost for European taxpayers; others worry long-range weapons could widen the war. Russia has not yet answered the U.S. talks proposal.

terms.explain: A bundle of money, weapons or supplies given to another country.
Fast drones with jet engines that are harder to shoot down than slow propeller ones.
Missiles, guns and radar that shoot down incoming drones and missiles.
Involving three sides — here the U.S., Ukraine and Russia.
The money used by Germany and most of the European Union.

stories.image_alt: Zelenskyy and Merz in front of a drone-damaged building in Kyiv

stories.headline: U.S. Marine arrested in killing of a woman on Okinawa; Japan protests
stories.dek: Tokyo summons the U.S. ambassador as old anger over American bases flares again.
stories.caveman: Police on Okinawa, Japan, arrested a 20-year-old U.S. Marine from the Futenma air station. He is suspected of killing a 39-year-old local woman in a hotel in Naha early Saturday (Oct. 3) and taking her wallet and backpack. Kyodo News said she appeared to have been strangled. Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja called it “absolutely unforgivable.” Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi protested to the U.S., and Foreign Minister Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass. About 50,000 U.S. troops are in Japan, roughly half of them on Okinawa.
stories.why_it_matters: Okinawa carries a heavy share of U.S. bases in Japan. Crimes by service members fuel calls to shrink the bases just as Tokyo wants closer military ties with the U.S. because of China.
stories.camps: Many Okinawans say they have lived for decades with noise, pollution and crime from the bases and want real change, not apologies. Japan’s national government and Washington see Okinawa as key to deterring China and focus on tougher discipline while keeping the alliance strong.

terms.explain: Japan’s southern island chain, home to about half the U.S. troops in Japan.
A U.S. Marine Corps air station in the middle of a crowded Okinawan city.
Officially called in to hear a complaint — a strong diplomatic signal.
A security partnership in which countries promise to help defend each other.
Rules and punishments that control how troops behave.

stories.image_alt: U.S. Osprey aircraft at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, Okinawa

stories.headline: October’s buzziest book: Barbara Kingsolver’s “Partita” tops every list
stories.dek: Book Riot crunched six major “most anticipated” lists; Orringer, Garmus and Schwab follow.
stories.caveman: Book Riot looked at six big October “most anticipated” lists — Goodreads, The New York Times, Bookshop.org, the Los Angeles Times, Barnes & Noble and Kirkus — to see which new books show up most. The winner: Barbara Kingsolver’s new novel “Partita,” which appeared on all six. Next came Julie Orringer’s “Luna, Phoenix, Queen” (five lists), then Bonnie Garmus’s “Peck & Peck” and V.E. Schwab’s “Victorious” (four each). Stephen Graham Jones’s “Off the Reservation,” T. Geronimo Johnson’s “The Occidental Book of the Dead,” Nathaniel Philbrick’s “The Rush,” and Chad Harbach’s “The Brightness” made three lists. Under-the-radar picks include Imbolo Mbue and Kawai Strong Washburn.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the fall “who’s hot” board. Kingsolver is coming off a Pulitzer for “Demon Copperhead,” and Garmus follows her megahit “Lessons in Chemistry,” so publishers are betting big.
stories.camps: Fans see a strong month mixing literary heavyweights, horror (Jones), fantasy (Schwab) and history (Philbrick). Critics of list culture note the same famous names get amplified everywhere, while smaller presses and debut writers struggle for attention.

terms.explain: Books readers and critics are most excited about before they come out.
Kirkus Reviews, a long-running U.S. book review magazine.
An online bookstore that shares profits with independent bookshops.
The Pulitzer Prize, a top American award for books and journalism.
A long, made-up story.

stories.image_alt: Grid of October 2026 new-release book covers

stories.headline: What America actually read in September: “The Correspondent” still rules Goodreads
stories.dek: Netflix pushes “The Love Hypothesis” into the top five; Marlon James and R.F. Kuang lead the critics’ buzz.
stories.caveman: Book Riot checked the most-read books on Goodreads in September. Most were carryovers from earlier months, led by Virginia Evans’s “The Correspondent” and Caro Claire Burke’s “Yesteryear.” A movie effect showed up fast: Netflix released its adaptation of Ali Hazelwood’s romance “The Love Hypothesis” late in the month, and that alone pushed it into the top five. Also on the list: Sally Hepworth’s “Mad Mabel” and Kathryn Stockett’s “The Calamity Club.” Book Riot pointed out the most-read list is not very diverse, so it highlighted buzzy September books by authors of color: Marlon James’s “The Disappearers,” which The New York Times called “the novel of the decade, if not the century,” R.F. Kuang’s “Taipei Story,” and Tananarive Due’s “Mazywood.”
stories.why_it_matters: This shows the gap between what critics rave about and what most people actually read — and how a streaming adaptation can still move books overnight.
stories.camps: Popular-taste fans say the list reflects real readers, who love cozy, emotional and romantic stories. Critics argue algorithms and marketing keep boosting the same kinds of books and authors, so writers of color need deliberate attention to be seen.

terms.explain: A big website where readers log and rate books; owned by Amazon.
Books that stayed popular from earlier months.
A movie or TV show made from a book.
Including people of different races, backgrounds and identities.
A genre focused on a love story, usually with a happy ending.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Virginia Evans’s novel The Correspondent

stories.headline: Audible will let you talk to book characters with AI — Lit Hub calls it “creepy”
stories.dek: New tools include live character guides and a chat feature piloting in an Audible Original “Dracula.”
stories.caveman: Audible, Amazon’s audiobook service, announced new AI-powered tools on Thursday (Oct. 1). One shows who is speaking in real time, so listeners don’t get lost; one gives spoiler-free character cards; another shows images and facts about places in the story. The most controversial: an interactive feature, powered by generative AI, that lets listeners ask questions as the story unfolds and even talk to characters. Amazon says that will appear only where the author allows it. The first test is a new Audible Original of Bram Stoker’s “Dracula,” which is in the public domain. A guide will also come to George Orwell’s “1984.” Literary Hub called the chat feature creepy.
stories.why_it_matters: AI is moving into how stories are told and sold. Writers worry about who controls their characters and words once a chatbot can speak for them.
stories.camps: Supporters say the tools help people who multitask or have memory or hearing challenges, and make classics more fun. Skeptics say the point of reading is the author’s voice and your own imagination, and fear starting with public-domain books is a first step toward using authors’ work more widely.

terms.explain: A book read aloud and recorded so you can listen to it.
AI that creates new text, images or voices on request.
Old works whose copyright has expired, so anyone can use them.
Information that reveals what happens later in a story.
A recording made and owned by Audible itself.

stories.image_alt: Lit Hub illustration about Audible’s AI character feature

stories.headline: NPR’s fall must-reads: Philyaw’s first novel, a Pitchfork memoir, and Dustin Hoffman
stories.dek: Ten picks mixing fiction, nonfiction and translations, from Kingsolver to a young-adult “Dirty Dancing.”
stories.caveman: NPR named 10 books it is excited about this fall. Fiction: Deesha Philyaw, whose 2020 story collection “The Secret Lives of Church Ladies” became a sensation from a small university press, finally has her first novel, “The True Confessions of First Lady Freeman” (out Sept. 29). Barbara Kingsolver’s “Partita” (Oct. 6) follows a pianist. Jasmine Guillory’s first young-adult novel, “It’s Only Dancing,” is a take on “Dirty Dancing.” Chad Harbach returns with “The Brightness” (Oct. 27). Nonfiction: Dustin Hoffman’s memoir “Look at Me” with Ariel Levy, Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber’s “Weird Era,” cartoonist Lisa Hanawalt, and science writer Olivia Judson. A translation of Mexican writer Amparo Dávila’s “Behind the Gate” (Nov. 3) and poems by Enrique Lihn round it out.
stories.why_it_matters: Fall is publishing’s biggest season. Lists like NPR’s help decide which books get attention before the holiday shopping rush.
stories.camps: Readers like that NPR mixes big names with smaller-press and translated books. Some critics say celebrity memoirs (like Hoffman’s) soak up attention that could go to lesser-known writers, though NPR argues they are part of the culture conversation too.

terms.explain: A book made of several short stories instead of one long novel.
A publisher run by a university, usually small and focused on serious books.
Books written mainly for teenage readers.
A true story someone writes about their own life.
Turned from another language into English.

stories.image_alt: Covers of books on NPR’s fall reading list

stories.headline: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passes 4,000 deaths; a treatment center is burned
stories.dek: The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record keeps spreading as unpaid health workers protest.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a deadly virus spread through body fluids. In eastern Congo, an outbreak declared on May 15 has now killed 4,018 people out of about 8,300 cases, the Health Ministry said — the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) says North Kivu province now has 40% of new confirmed cases; one coordinator said it is “like fighting a wildfire.” In Bunia, health workers protested because they have not been paid for months, with signs reading “No money, no data!” A U.N. official said soldiers searching for weapons burned a displacement camp that housed an Ebola transit center, forcing 19,000 people to flee. At least 50 health workers have died, and an infected MSF worker was flown to the Netherlands.
stories.why_it_matters: Ebola spreads where war, poverty and distrust meet. Every lost clinic and every unpaid worker gives the virus more room to spread, possibly across borders.
stories.camps: Aid groups and the U.N. say the world must send more money and protect health workers and clinics. Local communities, after years of conflict, often distrust outsiders and the government, which complicates the response; authorities have not explained the unpaid wages.

terms.explain: A severe, often deadly virus spread through contact with an infected person’s body fluids.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.
Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders), a global medical aid group.
A camp for people forced to flee their homes but still inside their country.
A place where possible patients are held and tested before treatment.

stories.image_alt: A health worker in protective gear is disinfected at an Ebola treatment center in Beni, Congo

stories.headline: Malaysia sends nearly 1,500 back to war-torn Myanmar despite U.N. warnings
stories.dek: Returnees arrive in Yangon on navy ships; rights groups fear persecution and forced conscription.
stories.caveman: On Sunday (Oct. 4), nearly 1,500 Myanmar citizens who had been held in Malaysia arrived in Yangon. They were deported and shipped back — a process called repatriation — on two navy warships and a hospital ship. They include 86 women. Malaysia plans to send back 5,000 in stages and holds 10,388 others in detention. The U.N. refugee agency and rights groups say Myanmar — in civil war since the military seized power in 2021 — is not safe; returnees could face persecution or be forced into the army. A U.N. rights expert pointed to non-refoulement — the rule against sending people back to danger — and said the risk is “substantial.” It is unclear if any are Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority.
stories.why_it_matters: Sending people back into a war zone can cost lives. It also tests whether countries keep the global rule against returning refugees to danger.
stories.camps: Malaysia treats them as immigration detainees it has the right to deport. The U.N. and rights groups say Malaysia must not send anyone back to persecution; Malaysia hosts about 215,600 refugees but has not signed the U.N. Refugee Convention and treats them as undocumented migrants.

terms.explain: Sent back to one’s home country.
International rule: you can’t send people back to a place where they face serious danger.
Being forced by the government to join the army.
A Muslim minority from Myanmar who have faced severe persecution and been denied citizenship.
A 1951 U.N. treaty that defines refugees and their rights.

stories.headline: Man deported by the U.S. to an African prison is freed after 14 months
stories.dek: Laotian Phone Chomsavanh had already served his U.S. sentence; his lawyer calls it a denial of due process.
stories.caveman: In July 2025, the U.S. deported five immigrants to Eswatini, a small kingdom in southern Africa where none of them had any ties. One of them, Phone Chomsavanh, a citizen of Laos, was released from a maximum-security prison there on Sunday (Oct. 4) after more than 14 months. He had been convicted of a crime in the U.S. but had already finished his sentence there. He was born in a refugee camp in Thailand and moved to the U.S. at age 7. His lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said what happened was “not due process by any definition.” He is now on his way to Laos. Eswatini was paid $5.1 million to take deportees.
stories.why_it_matters: This “third-country” program sends people to nations that are not their home, raising big questions about human rights and the rule of law.
stories.camps: The Trump administration says the program removes people with criminal records whose home countries won’t take them back quickly. Rights groups and lawyers say holding people who were never charged in those countries, without hearings, violates due process; around 500 people have been sent to African countries this way, advocates say.

terms.explain: Forced by a government to leave the country.
A country that is neither the person’s home nor the one deporting them.
Fair legal steps — notice, a hearing, a chance to argue — before the government punishes you.
A small country in southern Africa, ruled by a king; formerly called Swaziland.
A prison with the strictest guarding and limits.

stories.headline: “I am Jane Doe”: solidarity floods social media after Cornell rape lawsuit
stories.dek: Women post the name to shield an anonymous plaintiff — a wave many compare to #MeToo.
stories.caveman: A young woman has sued Cornell University and seven fraternity members, accusing them of raping her. She filed under the name “Jane Doe” to stay anonymous. After the college’s student newspaper reported on the lawsuit in late September, countless women began posting “I am Jane Doe” on social media. Many shared their own stories of sexual abuse. Part of the goal is protection: some people online have tried to find her real name, and posters hope the flood of “Jane Doe” posts will confuse search algorithms. Many say it feels like the height of #MeToo a decade ago. A law professor notes that using a pseudonym in lawsuits has grown, especially in very private cases. The claims have not been proven in court.
stories.why_it_matters: Sexual violence on campus is widespread and underreported. How survivors are protected — and how accused people get fair process — shapes whether others come forward.
stories.camps: Supporters say mass solidarity gives survivors courage and protects a woman from online harassment. Others stress that the people accused have not been found responsible by any court and deserve due process, and that public pressure should not replace a fair investigation.

terms.explain: A placeholder name used in court for a woman who wants to stay anonymous.
A fake name used instead of a real one.
A movement, big around 2017, where people shared experiences of sexual harassment and assault.
A social club for male college students in the U.S.
A case brought to court asking for a ruling or money.
